newsitem.title: UK: Flamboyant diarist Clark to make political comeback.
newsitem.headline: Flamboyant diarist Clark to make political comeback.

text.p: Raffish philanderer Alan Clark has an appetite for politics matched only by his libido.
Now, after landing the nomination to one of the safest and richest Conservative seats in parliament, the wealthy diarist with a sharp tongue and twinkling eye has promised to behave.

Gaffes abound in the flamboyant career of the former minister, who gave up his seat before the 1992 election, bitterly regretted the move and then staged a remarkable comeback on Thursday to land a plum London constituency.

"He's got much more experience than the rest, much more," said one elegant Conservative matron of a certain age when he took over Kensington and Chelsea from Sir Nicholas Scott, who was found lying in the gutter after a reception last year.
The 68-year-old Clark is an old-style Conservative with a taste for fine wines and fast cars.

He once made a speech to parliament when "not entirely sober" and admitted in his diary "We tasted first a bottle of Palmer 61, then for comparison a bottle of 75 Palmer, then switching back to a 61, a really delicious Pichon Longueville."
Quite open about his romantic conquests but still devoted to his long-suffering wife Jane, Clark once said: "Girls have to be succulent and under 25."
"I deserve to be horsewhipped" the former defence procurement minister said after a judge's wife claimed he had seduced her and her two daughters.
Clark called them "the coven" in his diary. His wife Jane said the three women displayed "below stairs behaviour".
But it was not just his love life that captured the headlines for Clark, who looks a certainty to return to parliament in the election due by May 22 at the latest.
Clark effectively brought the trial at the centre of a long-running affair over British arms exports to Iraq to a halt, by admitting that the government had been "economical with the actualite".
He inherited much of his estimated 40 million pound ($65 million) fortune from his father Kenneth Clark, famed for the landmark BBC television series "Civilisation".

A military historian who boasts an elegant family castle in southern England, he once witheringly labelled wealthy, self-made deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine as a man "who bought his own furniture".
He was fiercely loyal to former premier Margaret Thatcher who forgave his indiscretions and gave Clark trade, employment and defence portfolios in an eight-year ministerial career.
Clark said he found her attractive but then the notorious lady's man whose malicious and lecherous diaries outsold her own memoirs added swiftly: "I didn't want to jump on her." ($1=.6119 Pound)
